newsitem.title: UK: Bulgaria aims to sell six state banks in a year.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria aims to sell six state banks in a year.

text.p: Bulgaria aims to restore confidence in its deeply troubled banking system by privatising its leading six institutions by the middle of next year, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Bozhkov said on Sunday.

Bozhkov and other Bulgarian officials outlined an ambitious crash reform plan for banking and the shattered economy to the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) in London.
Bozhkov said confidence was returning to the Bulgarian economy in general following the recent signing of an agreement with the International Monetary Fund.

The economy was expected conservatively to have shrunk 4.8 percent last year but was beginning to recover in the second quarter of this year. The currency was stabilising and inflation falling to an expected 73 percent in the March-December period.
No former East Bloc nation has tried to privatise six leading banks so quickly since the 1989 fall of communism.
But Bozhkov said speed was essential in implementing long-delayed free-market reforms to take advantage of the current strong public support for the reformist government.

The interim government took power after street protests swept aside the Socialist administration of former communists in February. Elections are due to be held on April 19 and the reformist Union of Democratic Forces and its allies are favourites to win a majority in parliament.
"We aim to boost confidence (in the banking system) with the privatisation of two state banks by the end of September 1997," Bozhkov told bankers from East and West at an EBRD presentation.

Agreements to sell two further banks would be reached by the end of this year and the remaining two by the end of June next year. The aim was to come from "a state-dominated banking system to a sound private banking system by the end of 1998".
Asked which banks would be sold first, he said: "Which will be privatised depends on which are wanted".

But a top official of the Bulgarian Bank Consolidation Company, which will play a leading role in the privatisation, said talks were underway with the EBRD about the London based-development bank taking a stake in United Bulgarian Bank (UBB).

Chief executive director Valentin Tsvetanov told Reuters that investors had also shown interest in buying Expressbank, which based in the city of Varna. The other state banks earmarked for sale included Biochimbank, the Bulgarian Postbank and Hebrosbank, which is based in Plovdiv.

Tsvetanov said that the preferred privatisation method was a bidding process and any investor, domestic or foreign, could buy into the banks. There was no limit on what percentage could be bought. But talks on a direct sale of UBB were at a "very mature stage" and he hoped a deal could be sealed by the end of June.
Under its rules, the EBRD cannot take more than 35 percent of UBB, meaning private investors would also be needed for full privatisation to happen.
Bulgarian banking is deep in crisis. Insolvency cases are pending against 14 banks and panicked depositors withdrew nearly $1 billion in deposits last year.
The previous Socialist government also spoke of implementing wide economic reforms but shied away from action due to the pain it would inflict on an already impoverished population.

Bozhkov admitted the new government's plans, which he said would continue after the elections, would cause further pain. But he said it was vital to move fast while public support was high. President Petar Stoyanov had 90 percent support and the government more than 60 percent, he said.
"In the history of the transition in Bulgaria there hasn't been a government with such a high degree of support," he said, adding: "If we are slow we will be wiped out."

Sally Warren, an EBRD consultant on financial institutions, said she optimistic that two banks including UBB could be sold by the middle of this year. But she added: "I think the deadline of six by the end of 1998 is optimistic."
But Bozhov dismissed suggestions that reform had been delayed too long in Bulgaria. "We are late, but we are good," he said.
